ann_48.text: This part gives every square a fixed value and adds them up, counting a piece for x when x holds it and against x when o holds it.

Central low squares count most for x: for the typical position, an x piece on d3 raises the predicted chance that x wins in an uneven way, from about 74% to about 95%, and an x piece on d4 to about 90%.
Swapping an o piece for an x piece on c3 raises it in an uneven way from about 48% to about 90%, and on d2 from about 51% to about 88%.
Squares on the edge columns count against their owner: swapping an o piece for an x piece on a1 lowers it in an uneven way from about 90% to about 47%, and on g1 from about 90% to about 47%.
The top row counts against its owner too: an x piece on g6 lowers it steadily from about 74% to about 19%, flattening out near the top because the predicted chance cannot go much higher.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 54045 training positions.

ann_49.text: This part acts on 38646 of 54045 training positions (72%), every position where o does not hold square c1.
For the typical position it acts on, it lowers the predicted chance that x wins from about 78% without it to about 64% with it.

Through this part, square c1 lowers the predicted chance only from empty upwards, slowly at first, then faster: for the typical position, from about 77% with an o piece on c1 to about 63% with an x piece there.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 54045 training positions.

ann_50.text: This part lowers the predicted chance that x wins with nothing until x holds square b6, then steadily: for the typical position, from about 74% to about 69%.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 54045 training positions.

ann_51.text: This part acts on 12765 of 54045 training positions (24%), nearly all of them positions where x holds square f1.
For the typical position it acts on, it raises the predicted chance that x wins from about 46% without it to about 58% with it.

Swapping an o piece for an x piece on b1 lowers the predicted chance in an uneven way, and even more so if x holds f1: for the typical position, from about 81% to about 44% if x holds f1, and from about 85% to about 59% if not.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 54045 training positions.

ann_52.text: The model adds up four parts: a value for every square, and three small corrections for squares c1, f1 and b6.
An x piece on d3 raises the predicted chance that x wins in an uneven way, from about 74% to about 95% for the typical position.
An x piece on the top row lowers it steadily: on g6 from about 74% to about 19%, on b6 to about 22%, on c6 to about 28%.
Swapping an o piece for an x piece on a1 lowers it in an uneven way from about 90% to about 47%.
It ignores squares b3, d5, e4, f3 and f4.

ann_48.original: Linear backbone: a fixed value per square, counted for x and against x for o. identity_0 = sum_s w_s*z_s over 36 squares; per raw piece (x on the square vs empty; o is the exact negative) the values are, top row first: row6: a6 -1.87 b6 -2.05 c6 -1.97 d6 -1.37 e6 +0.00 f6 -2.45 g6 -2.47; row5: a5 -1.42 b5 -1.11 c5 -0.84 d5 +0.00 e5 -1.32 f5 -1.33 g5 -1.62; row4: a4 -0.87 b4 +0.11 c4 +0.46 d4 +1.14 e4 +0.00 f4 +0.00 g4 -0.94; row3: a3 -1.09 b3 +0.00 c3 +1.11 d3 +2.01 e3 +0.91 f3 +0.00 g3 -1.18; row2: a2 -1.15 b2 +0.18 c2 +0.49 d2 +1.00 e2 +0.38 f2 +0.06 g2 -1.22; row1: a1 -1.17 b1 -0.69 c1 +0.05 d1 +0.36 e1 -0.69 f1 -0.73 g1 -1.14 (b3, d5, e4, f3, f4 unconnected, value 0). Because each side always has exactly 4 pieces, only differences between squares matter. Domain reading: material weighted by square quality. Central low squares are worth most (d3 +2.01, d4 +1.14, c3 +1.11, d2 +1.00, e3 +0.91); edge columns a and g (-0.9 to -2.5) and the top rows 5-6 (-0.8 to -2.5) are worth least, i.e. an x piece there counts against x and an o piece there for x. Evidence (training split, 54,045 rows): corr 0.81 with the classic count of winning lines through each square (0.94 on rows 1-3). A fit value = -1.75 + 0.24*lines + 0.14*odd_row - 0.27*edge_column - 1.09*(row 5 or 6) gives R2 0.91 against 0.70 for lines alone. Departures from the line count: rows 5-6 are penalised as a block (lines say row 6 = row 1); row 3 outranks row 4 (centre mean +1.34 vs +0.80, though they lie on equally many lines), a small effect in the direction of x's odd-row preference; edges sit below their line value. These departures are in the data: corr 0.93 with the per-square marginal empirical log-odds (x on it vs o on it), corr 0.96 with an ordinal logistic regression's coefficients. Line-count-weighted material alone ranks wins with AUC 0.821 (network 0.858) and correlates 0.90 with the logit. Linear by construction (restore gain 0). Assessment: meaningful (a weighted-material evaluation close to the line-count heuristic); the top-row block penalty has no domain explanation here.
ann_48.proposed: Gives every square a fixed value: central low squares count for whoever holds them in an uneven way, edge columns in an uneven way and the top rows steadily against their owner.

ann_49.original: Per-value correction at square c1. 4277 = relu(1.114*z(c1) + 0.680): 0 when o holds c1 (15,399 rows), 0.43 when c1 is empty (13,007), 1.74 when x holds c1 (25,639); it enters the logit with weight -0.390. With the direct c1 edge (+0.054 per piece) the c1 effect vs empty is x -0.46, o +0.11 logit: unlike every other square, x and o are not mirror images on c1. Since square values are fixed only up to a per-player constant, centred values are compared: network x +0.09, o -0.47; a one-hot logistic regression (separate x and o value per square) gives x -0.00, o -0.52. So the hinge reproduces a real asymmetry in the data: an o piece on c1 helps o by about half a logit relative to an average square, an x piece on c1 is worth an average square to x (marginal P(win): c1 = o 0.680, empty 0.663, x 0.643). Restore gain 0.0002 AUC (linearised alone: 0.8573 vs 0.8576). Assessment: closed-form-only. The statement is data-faithful, but no domain concept (lines through c1 = 5, centre, threats, odd/even rows) explains why c1 should be asymmetric; it restates the formula in board terms. c1 is also not the largest x/o asymmetry in the data (d3, d2, b2 are larger and are left linear).
ann_49.proposed: Lowers the predicted chance that x wins unless o holds square c1, slowly at first, then faster, so most when x holds it.

ann_50.original: Rare-square correction at b6 (top of column b). 3400 = relu(0.916*z(b6) - 1.457) fires only when x holds b6 (119 of 54,045 rows; value 8.95, z(b6 = x) = 11.4 because b6 is almost always empty); 4423 = relu(0.949*3400 + 0.659) is an always-on relay (constant 0.659 otherwise). Into the logit with weight -0.027: x on b6 costs an extra 0.23 logit on top of the direct b6 value (-2.06 per piece), so x on b6 totals -2.29 vs o on b6 +2.05. On the 119 rows P(win) is 0.395; mean prediction 0.377 with the hinge, 0.417 without, so it neither helps nor hurts calibration materially. Restore gain 5e-6 AUC. ann_51.original: Flank correction at f1, damped by x on b1. 180 = relu(1.064*z(f1) - 0.234*z(e6) + 0.519*2268 - 0.296*4093 - 1.578), into the logit with +0.328. 1824 and 2268 are always on (linear relays carrying a constant 1.36 plus a tiny a4 term, +-0.12 when a4 is held). 4093 = relu(3.186*z(b1) + 1.0*z(e6) - 0.283) is an indicator of 'x holds b1' (3.27; 0 otherwise) except on the 67 rows with a piece on e6, where the huge z(e6) dominates. Effects: it softens the direct f1 value for x (x on f1 vs empty: -0.78 direct, -0.27 in total) so f1 is no longer mirror-symmetric; centred network values x +0.15 / o +0.14 vs one-hot regression +0.13 / +0.20. The b1 damping is an interaction: x on both b1 and f1 lowers the logit by 0.32 beyond the two single-square values; a regression with one-hot square values plus a [b1 = x and f1 = x] term finds -0.33 (n = 4,467). So both effects are in the data. No four-cell line contains both b1 and f1. Restore gain 0.0007 AUC (the largest of the three hinges). ann_52.original: Root: the win logit is additive. logit = 1.341 + board_material_weights - 0.390*c1_owner_hinge - 0.027*b6_top_hinge + 0.328*f1_edge_hinge; P(x wins) = sigmoid(logit). parts.name: board_material_weights
parts.original_hypothesis: Linear backbone: a fixed value per square, counted for x and against x for o. identity_0 = sum_s w_s*z_s over 36 squares; per raw piece (x on the square vs empty; o is the exact negative) the values are, top row first: row6: a6 -1.87 b6 -2.05 c6 -1.97 d6 -1.37 e6 +0.00 f6 -2.45 g6 -2.47; row5: a5 -1.42 b5 -1.11 c5 -0.84 d5 +0.00 e5 -1.32 f5 -1.33 g5 -1.62; row4: a4 -0.87 b4 +0.11 c4 +0.46 d4 +1.14 e4 +0.00 f4 +0.00 g4 -0.94; row3: a3 -1.09 b3 +0.00 c3 +1.11 d3 +2.01 e3 +0.91 f3 +0.00 g3 -1.18; row2: a2 -1.15 b2 +0.18 c2 +0.49 d2 +1.00 e2 +0.38 f2 +0.06 g2 -1.22; row1: a1 -1.17 b1 -0.69 c1 +0.05 d1 +0.36 e1 -0.69 f1 -0.73 g1 -1.14 (b3, d5, e4, f3, f4 unconnected, value 0). Because each side always has exactly 4 pieces, only differences between squares matter. Domain reading: material weighted by square quality. Central low squares are worth most (d3 +2.01, d4 +1.14, c3 +1.11, d2 +1.00, e3 +0.91); edge columns a and g (-0.9 to -2.5) and the top rows 5-6 (-0.8 to -2.5) are worth least, i.e. an x piece there counts against x and an o piece there for x. Evidence (training split, 54,045 rows): corr 0.81 with the classic count of winning lines through each square (0.94 on rows 1-3). A fit value = -1.75 + 0.24*lines + 0.14*odd_row - 0.27*edge_column - 1.09*(row 5 or 6) gives R2 0.91 against 0.70 for lines alone. Departures from the line count: rows 5-6 are penalised as a block (lines say row 6 = row 1); row 3 outranks row 4 (centre mean +1.34 vs +0.80, though they lie on equally many lines), a small effect in the direction of x's odd-row preference; edges sit below their line value. These departures are in the data: corr 0.93 with the per-square marginal empirical log-odds (x on it vs o on it), corr 0.96 with an ordinal logistic regression's coefficients. Line-count-weighted material alone ranks wins with AUC 0.821 (network 0.858) and correlates 0.90 with the logit. Linear by construction (restore gain 0). Assessment: meaningful (a weighted-material evaluation close to the line-count heuristic); the top-row block penalty has no domain explanation here.

parts.name: c1_owner_hinge
parts.original_hypothesis: Per-value correction at square c1. 4277 = relu(1.114*z(c1) + 0.680): 0 when o holds c1 (15,399 rows), 0.43 when c1 is empty (13,007), 1.74 when x holds c1 (25,639); it enters the logit with weight -0.390. With the direct c1 edge (+0.054 per piece) the c1 effect vs empty is x -0.46, o +0.11 logit: unlike every other square, x and o are not mirror images on c1. Since square values are fixed only up to a per-player constant, centred values are compared: network x +0.09, o -0.47; a one-hot logistic regression (separate x and o value per square) gives x -0.00, o -0.52. So the hinge reproduces a real asymmetry in the data: an o piece on c1 helps o by about half a logit relative to an average square, an x piece on c1 is worth an average square to x (marginal P(win): c1 = o 0.680, empty 0.663, x 0.643). Restore gain 0.0002 AUC (linearised alone: 0.8573 vs 0.8576). Assessment: closed-form-only. The statement is data-faithful, but no domain concept (lines through c1 = 5, centre, threats, odd/even rows) explains why c1 should be asymmetric; it restates the formula in board terms. c1 is also not the largest x/o asymmetry in the data (d3, d2, b2 are larger and are left linear).

parts.name: f1_edge_hinge
parts.original_hypothesis: Flank correction at f1, damped by x on b1. 180 = relu(1.064*z(f1) - 0.234*z(e6) + 0.519*2268 - 0.296*4093 - 1.578), into the logit with +0.328. 1824 and 2268 are always on (linear relays carrying a constant 1.36 plus a tiny a4 term, +-0.12 when a4 is held). 4093 = relu(3.186*z(b1) + 1.0*z(e6) - 0.283) is an indicator of 'x holds b1' (3.27; 0 otherwise) except on the 67 rows with a piece on e6, where the huge z(e6) dominates. Effects: it softens the direct f1 value for x (x on f1 vs empty: -0.78 direct, -0.27 in total) so f1 is no longer mirror-symmetric; centred network values x +0.15 / o +0.14 vs one-hot regression +0.13 / +0.20. The b1 damping is an interaction: x on both b1 and f1 lowers the logit by 0.32 beyond the two single-square values; a regression with one-hot square values plus a [b1 = x and f1 = x] term finds -0.33 (n = 4,467). So both effects are in the data. No four-cell line contains both b1 and f1. Restore gain 0.0007 AUC (the largest of the three hinges). Assessment: closed-form-only; data-faithful corrections (an f1 asymmetry and a b1-f1 'two flank moves' interaction) without a line, threat or centre concept behind them.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording
